disclaimer: This report is for educational and wellness purposes only. It is not a medical diagnosis and does not replace advice from a qualified healthcare professional. HbA1c results should be confirmed by your doctor. Do not start, stop or change any medication without medical advice.

status.label: In the prediabetes range
status.explanation: Your HbA1c is between 5.7% and 6.4%, the range used for prediabetes. This is a common and often reversible stage where lifestyle changes make the biggest difference.

summary: Your HbA1c is in the prediabetes range, which means this is a good time to make changes before things progress further. Your BMI falls in the obese range, and combined with low physical activity, regular alcohol use, and your age, this adds to your overall risk. Your sleep apnoea and weight also play an important role in blood sugar patterns, so addressing them together can help. The most valuable next steps are keeping up with your highlighted HbA1c and liver checks, building in regular gentle activity, and following your calorie target and meal constraints closely.

comorbidity_assessment.note: Poor sleep quality from untreated sleep apnoea can make blood sugar harder to manage and may worsen insulin resistance over time. Using any prescribed breathing support consistently and keeping a steady sleep schedule can help support healthier glucose patterns.

Carrying extra weight, especially around the middle, is closely linked to higher blood sugar levels and insulin resistance. Gradual, steady weight loss can ease pressure on both your blood sugar control and your sleep apnoea.

constraints: Avoid alcohol and heavy meals within 3 hours of bedtime.
Follow the calorie target; avoid sugary drinks and fruit juices completely.
Fill half the plate with non-starchy vegetables to stay full on fewer calories.

foods_to_eat: Non-starchy vegetables like zucchini, spinach, peppers, and tomatoes
Whole grains such as bulgur, farro, and whole grain bread in small portions
Legumes like chickpeas, lentils, and beans
Fatty fish such as salmon, sardines, and mackerel
Olive oil as the main cooking fat
Nuts and seeds in small handfuls
Plain yogurt and small amounts of cheese like feta
foods_to_avoid: Refined flour products like white bread and pastries
Sweets and desserts with added sugar
Processed meats like sausages and bacon
Large heavy meals close to bedtime
plan.portion_guidance: Fill half your plate with non-starchy vegetables, a quarter with lean protein like fish, chicken, or legumes, and a quarter with whole grains. Use household measures like a bowl or katori to keep portions consistent and avoid overeating, which supports your calorie target of 1,850 kcal.
plan.hydration: Aim for 8 to 10 glasses of water through the day. Herbal tea and plain sparkling water are good choices. Avoid sugary drinks and limit alcohol, especially in the evening since it can affect sleep quality and blood sugar.
based_on: obesity: focus on vegetables and portion control
sleep apnoea: avoid heavy meals and alcohol before bedtime
regular alcohol use: limit and avoid near bedtime

exercise: Start with gentle, low-impact activities such as short walks, stationary cycling, or water-based exercise to protect your joints, especially given your weight and sedentary history.
Gradually build toward at least 150 minutes a week of moderate activity, adding a few minutes every week as your fitness improves.
Include muscle-strengthening activities on 2 days a week, such as light resistance bands or bodyweight exercises.
Avoid pushing into vigorous exercise too quickly; progress slowly and listen to your body.
lifestyle.walking_goal: Begin with 10-minute walks, 5 days a week, and build up gradually to 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week, as comfort and stamina allow.
lifestyle.weight_management: Your BMI is in the obese range, and gradual weight loss of about 5–10% of your body weight over the next 6 months can help reduce the severity of sleep apnoea and support healthier blood sugar levels. Focus on steady, sustainable changes to eating and activity rather than quick fixes, and track progress weekly rather than daily.
lifestyle.sleep: Keep a regular sleep and wake schedule, even on weekends, and use any prescribed breathing device every night without exception. Create a calm pre-sleep routine, limit screens before bed, and aim for 7 to 9 hours of sleep. If you notice loud snoring, gasping, or daytime tiredness, mention this to a healthcare provider.
stress: Practice slow, deep breathing exercises for 5–10 minutes daily to help calm your nervous system.
Try progressive muscle relaxation or a short daily mindfulness practice to manage stress.
Consider gentle activities like walking or stretching, which can also help release tension.
behaviour_change: Since you drink regularly, consider cutting down gradually — try setting alcohol-free days each week and tracking your intake to notice patterns.
As a former smoker, staying smoke-free is a great achievement; if you ever feel at risk of returning to smoking, reach out to a quitline or your doctor for support.
Build small, consistent habits such as planning meals ahead and setting a regular bedtime to support long-term change.
Celebrate small wins along the way, like consistent walks or improved sleep routines, to stay motivated.
based_on: Goal of gradual weight loss of 5-10% over 6 months
Need to protect joints when starting activity

monitoring.name: HbA1c
monitoring.why: Catches progression from prediabetes to diabetes early.

monitoring.name: Liver check (liver tests and FIB-4 score)
monitoring.why: Fatty liver is common with diabetes and obesity and can progress without symptoms.
monitoring.frequency: FIB-4 score every 1–2 years, or sooner if your doctor finds a higher risk

monitoring.name: Fasting blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows your blood glucose after an overnight fast and complements HbA1c.
monitoring.frequency: Alongside your HbA1c test, or as your doctor advises

monitoring.name: Vitamin D
monitoring.why: Low vitamin D is more common with obesity and kidney disease; testing is not routine for everyone.
monitoring.frequency: Only if your doctor recommends it

monitoring.name: Blood pressure
monitoring.why: High blood pressure multiplies the heart and kidney risks of high blood glucose.
monitoring.frequency: At every doctor visit; at home regularly if you have high blood pressure

preventive_actions: Schedule your highlighted HbA1c and liver function tests (including FIB-4) as recommended.
Start physical activity gently, such as short walks, and build up slowly to protect your joints.
Follow your calorie target of 1850 calories and fill half your plate with non-starchy vegetables.
Avoid alcohol and heavy meals within three hours of bedtime to support better sleep and glucose control.
Aim for gradual weight loss of about 5–10% of your body weight over six months.
Keep a consistent sleep schedule and use any prescribed breathing device every night.
